**Vignette: Gerald, Age 70**

Gerald has spent the better part of forty years on the road. He knows how to read a room, how to put a stranger at ease within the first thirty seconds of a handshake, how to close a deal over a cup of coffee in a diner booth. Selling agricultural equipment across the rural Midwest has been his life's work, and he has always taken quiet pride in the fact that he could walk into any situation and find his footing. That confidence, he says, is mostly gone now.

Fourteen months ago, Gerald was returning to his car after a late-afternoon client meeting in a mid-sized city he had visited dozens of times before. The parking garage was quieter than usual. Two men approached him from behind, demanded his keys and wallet, and when he hesitated — more out of shock than defiance — one of them struck him across the face and shoved him hard against the concrete pillar. He went down. He remembers the cold of the ground, the sound of his own breathing, and the feeling that he had no idea whether they were going to stop. They took what they wanted and ran. The physical injuries were relatively minor — a cut above his eye, bruised ribs — but Gerald lay on that garage floor for several minutes before he could make himself stand up.

In the weeks that followed, he told his wife, Donna, that he was fine. He went back to work. He drove his routes. But something had quietly reorganized itself inside him. He began avoiding parking garages entirely, rerouting his schedule in ways he didn't fully explain to his clients or his manager. He started parking only in open lots, in daylight, as close to building entrances as possible. When that wasn't possible, he would sit in his car for long stretches, watching the mirrors, telling himself he was just checking his phone.

Sleep became unreliable. He wakes most nights between two and three in the morning, heart already going, the details of the garage vivid and immediate — the footsteps behind him, the impact, the ground. He doesn't always know what pulls him out of sleep, but once he's awake, the memory tends to find him. Donna has noticed, though Gerald deflects when she asks. He doesn't want to worry her, and he's also not entirely sure how to explain that a man who has navigated thirty years of cold calls and difficult clients is now struggling to walk through a parking lot without scanning every shadow.

At work, he finds himself irritable in ways that feel foreign to him. He has always prided himself on patience — it's a prerequisite in sales — but lately small frustrations ignite something disproportionate. A client who keeps him waiting, a slow elevator, a colleague who crowds his personal space without thinking. He snaps, then feels ashamed of it. He has started turning down evening appointments, which is costing him. His manager has noticed the dip in his numbers.

Gerald describes a persistent sense that the world has a different texture now. He used to feel, without quite articulating it, that things were basically manageable. That feeling is harder to locate. He finds himself thinking about retirement differently — not as something to look forward to but as something he needs to get to, a kind of safety. He and Donna had planned to travel when he finally stepped back from work. He doesn't say so directly, but when the subject comes up, he changes it.

What strikes Gerald most, and what he returns to across conversations, is the loss of something he can't quite name — a ease in his own body, a basic assumption that he could handle whatever came at him. He built a career on that assumption. He's not sure, at seventy, how to rebuild it, or whether he's supposed to try.
